276eef8e2d22f6e225440f49dfeb3de246f91df1.summary: Rapid7 report (published 2025-06-10) on social engineering attacks that start with email bombing, then fake help desk calls via Microsoft Teams or phone, then remote access tools such as Quick Assist. It says BlackSuit affiliates appear to have adopted Black Basta's approach after Black Basta's internal conflict. It describes a Java RAT that uses Google cloud services for command and control, a QEMU virtual machine delivery method with the QDoor proxy, and a Rust loader. It assesses that some access may be sold to other groups.

hedges: Evidence now suggests that BlackSuit affiliates have either adopted Black Basta's strategy or absorbed members of the group.
The developer(s) of the Java malware family are assessed as likely initial access brokers, potentially having provided access for Black Basta and/or FIN7 affiliates.
The threat actor may not be intending to use the access for themselves, but rather sell it to another group, according to the report's reading of the behaviour.
The test lab is most likely also the environment in which the threat actor compiled testapp.exe.
The report says the BlackSuit and Black Basta connection is shown by the chat leaks, and the adaptation of their spear phishing is unsurprising.
QDoor's attribution to the BlackSuit ransomware group is made by ConnectWise, as cited in the report.
The python RAT naming as Anubis is described as likely based on the source code; the FIN7 attribution is from GData, as cited in the report.
